source_title: My heart is like a singing bird
candidate_text:
A morning opened like a bright window,
and every small thing seemed newly made.
The orchard stirred with blossom and birds;
a clear stream carried the day's gladness.
I gathered no flower from the field,
but watched their colors fill the air.
A loved one crossed the garden path,
and ordinary hours became a feast.

source_title: My heart is like a singing bird
candidate_text:
My joy began when you arrived.
The garden seemed to brighten,
the fruit trees bowed beneath their harvest,
and birds filled the quiet air.
I wanted to dress the room in color,
to set bright flowers beside the door,
and make this ordinary day memorable.
Your presence turned it into a celebration.

Rain threads the roofs throughout the afternoon,
and bare branches tremble beside the lane.
The fields look tired beneath the clouds,
while distant hills disappear in gray.
Still, somewhere beyond this weather,
a warmer season waits beyond our sight.
I keep a little hope beside the lamp
and let the passing storm move on.

The weather is bleak today;
rain keeps falling and the trees bend.
Old leaves gather along the wall,
and the road is dark beneath the clouds.
My thoughts feel much the same:
plans have faded and hope seems distant.
But clouds do not remain forever;
somewhere above them, daylight continues.

source_text:
The shades of night were falling fast,
As through an Alpine village passed
A youth, who bore, 'mid snow and ice,
A banner with the strange device,
       Excelsior!

His brow was sad; his eye beneath,
Flashed like a falchion from its sheath,
And like a silver clarion rung
The accents of that unknown tongue,
       Excelsior!

In happy homes he saw the light
Of household fires gleam warm and bright;
Above, the spectral glaciers shone,
And from his lips escaped a groan,
       Excelsior!

"Try not the Pass!" the old man said:
"Dark lowers the tempest overhead,
The roaring torrent is deep and wide!
And loud that clarion voice replied,
       Excelsior!

"Oh stay," the maiden said, "and rest
Thy weary head upon this breast!"
A tear stood in his bright blue eye,
But still he answered, with a sigh,
       Excelsior!

"Beware the pine-tree's withered branch!
Beware the awful avalanche!"
This was the peasant's last Good-night,
A voice replied, far up the height,
        Excelsior!

At break of day, as heavenward
The pious monks of Saint Bernard
Uttered the oft-repeated prayer,
A voice cried through the startled air,
       Excelsior!

A traveller, by the faithful hound,
Half-buried in the snow was found,
Still grasping in his hand of ice
That banner with the strange device,
       Excelsior!

There in the twilight cold and gray,
Lifeless, but beautiful, he lay,
And from the sky, serene and far,
A voice fell, like a falling star,
       Excelsior!
candidate_text:
A lone traveler climbed toward the pass
while winter gathered over the peaks.
Villagers called him back to shelter,
but a distant summit held his gaze.
He crossed the narrow bridge at dusk,
following a dream no one could share.
By dawn, the trail had vanished under snow;
only his footprints marked the upward road.

candidate_text:
Night was descending over the mountain village
when a young traveler began the climb.
He carried a bright flag and a stubborn hope,
though the snow made every step uncertain.
People offered shelter and warned of danger;
he thanked them but continued upward.
The storm erased the path behind him.
At sunrise, the valley found him still,
his journey ended beneath the silent peaks.

source_text:
ONE of my wishes is that those dark trees,
    So old and firm they scarcely show the breeze,
    Were not, as 'twere, the merest mask of gloom,
    But stretched away unto the edge of doom.
    I should not be withheld but that some day
    Into their vastness I should steal away,
    Fearless of ever finding open land,
    Or highway where the slow wheel pours the sand.
    I do not see why I should e'er turn back,
    Or those should not set forth upon my track
    To overtake me, who should miss me here
    And long to know if still I held them dear.
    They would not find me changed from him they knew--
    Only more sure of all I thought was true.
candidate_text:
Beyond the familiar orchard lies a country
I have imagined but never entered.
The old trees hide its distant border,
their branches whispering of open ground.
Perhaps I will leave before the next rain,
with no map folded in my coat.
Those who know me may follow later;
I hope they understand why I went.

candidate_text:
I often imagine leaving these familiar woods,
walking until the known roads disappear.
The trees stand like a dark boundary,
but beyond them there may be open country.
I would go without fear of turning back,
even if those at home wondered where I was.
They might search the distant paths
and find that I had kept my purpose.

source_text:
I DWELL in a lonely house I know
    That vanished many a summer ago,
    And left no trace but the cellar walls,
    And a cellar in which the daylight falls,
    And the purple-stemmed wild raspberries grow.
    O'er ruined fences the grape-vines shield
    The woods come back to the mowing field;
    The orchard tree has grown one copse
    Of new wood and old where the woodpecker chops;
    The footpath down to the well is healed.
    I dwell with a strangely aching heart
    In that vanished abode there far apart
    On that disused and forgotten road
    That has no dust-bath now for the toad.
    Night comes; the black bats tumble and dart;
    The whippoorwill is coming to shout
    And hush and cluck and flutter about:
    I hear him begin far enough away
    Full many a time to say his say
    Before he arrives to say it out.
    It is under the small, dim, summer star.
    I know not who these mute folk are
    Who share the unlit place with me--
    Those stones out under the low-limbed tree
    Doubtless bear names that the mosses mar.
    They are tireless folk, but slow and sad,
    Though two, close-keeping, are lass and lad,--
    With none among them that ever sings,
    And yet, in view of how many things,
    As sweet companions as might be had.
candidate_text:
At the edge of the meadow stands
a house remembered by the oldest trees.
Its roof has fallen into the grass,
and wild vines cover the garden gate.
No voices rise from its rooms now,
yet evening seems to gather there.
I walk past slowly, listening
for the lives that once filled it.

candidate_text:
I know a house that time has emptied.
Its walls have fallen and grass covers the floor;
wild berries grow where the doorway stood.
The orchard has become part of the woods,
and the old path is nearly gone.
At night, bats cross the broken roof.
I feel the presence of forgotten lives
among the stones beneath the trees.

source_text:
MY Sorrow, when she's here with me,
    Thinks these dark days of autumn rain
    Are beautiful as days can be;
    She loves the bare, the withered tree;
    She walks the sodden pasture lane.
    Her pleasure will not let me stay.
    She talks and I am fain to list:
    She's glad the birds are gone away,
    She's glad her simple worsted gray
    Is silver now with clinging mist.
    The desolate, deserted trees,
    The faded earth, the heavy sky,
    The beauties she so truly sees,
    She thinks I have no eye for these,
    And vexes me for reason why.
    Not yesterday I learned to know
    The love of bare November days
    Before the coming of the snow,
    But it were vain to tell her so,
    And they are better for her praise.
candidate_text:
November lays a silver veil on fields,
and quiet birds depart before the frost.
The empty branches make a gentle pattern
against the pale and lowering sky.
I used to call this season sorrowful;
today its stillness feels like rest.
The world grows simple as it darkens,
and I begin to understand its beauty.

She finds loveliness in the late autumn,
when rain darkens the fields and trees stand bare.
The birds have left, the ground is faded,
and mist rests on the branches.
I once saw only loss in this season,
but her patient gaze changed mine.
Now I understand the quiet beauty
that arrives just before winter.

source_text:
The sun does arise,
   And make happy the skies;
   The merry bells ring
   To welcome the Spring;
   The skylark and thrush,
   The birds of the bush,
   Sing louder around
   To the bells' cheerful sound;
   While our sports shall be seen
   On the echoing Green.

   Old John, with white hair,
   Does laugh away care,
   Sitting under the oak,
   Among the old folk.
   They laugh at our play,
   And soon they all say,
   "Such, such were the joys
   When we all--girls and boys--
   In our youth-time were seen
   On the echoing Green."

   Till the little ones, weary,
   No more can be merry:
   The sun does descend,
   And our sports have an end.
   Round the laps of their mothers
   Many sisters and brothers,
   Like birds in their nest,
   Are ready for rest,
   And sport no more seen
   On the darkening green.
candidate_text:
Children race beneath the morning sun,
their laughter scattering across the common.
Old neighbors watch beside the gate
and trade stories of their younger days.
The afternoon grows soft and golden;
one by one the games fall quiet.
At dusk, small hands find their families,
and the green returns to silence.

The morning sun wakes the village,
and children gather on the common.
Bells ring while birds sing from the hedges;
the old people smile at the games.
They remember their own bright summers
as the young ones run across the grass.
When evening comes, the children grow tired,
and the green field settles into dusk.

source_text:
Little Lamb, who made thee
     Dost thou know who made thee,
   Gave thee life, and bid thee feed
   By the stream and o'er the mead;
   Gave thee clothing of delight,
   Softest clothing, woolly, bright;
   Gave thee such a tender voice,
   Making all the vales rejoice?
     Little Lamb, who made thee?
     Dost thou know who made thee?

     Little Lamb, I'll tell thee;
     Little Lamb, I'll tell thee:
   He is called by thy name,
   For He calls Himself a Lamb
   He is meek, and He is mild,
   He became a little child.
   I a child, and thou a lamb,
   We are called by His name.
     Little Lamb, God bless thee!
     Little Lamb, God bless thee!
candidate_text:
A small creature grazes by the brook,
its fleece bright in the open light.
Who taught it to find the tender grass,
or gave its quiet voice such peace?
A child kneels near the water's edge
and watches it without a sound.
The world seems gentle for a moment,
as kindness moves between them.

A lamb rests beside the stream.
It feeds among the soft meadow grass,
and its coat shines in the afternoon.
A child asks who gave it life,
who made its voice so gentle.
The answer is found in tenderness:
the small and the young are precious,
and care should surround them.

source_text:
In a world of moan,
          And my soul was a stagnant tide,
  Till the fair and gentle Eulalie became my blushing bride—
  Till the yellow-haired young Eulalie became my smiling bride.

              Ah, less—less bright
              The stars of the night
  Than the eyes of the radiant girl!
              And never a flake
              That the vapour can make
  With the moon-tints of purple and pearl,
  Can vie with the modest Eulalie’s most unregarded curl—
  Can compare with the bright-eyed Eulalie’s most humble and careless curl.

              Now Doubt—now Pain
              Come never again,
          For her soul gives me sigh for sigh,
              And all day long
              Shines, bright and strong,
          Astarte within the sky,
  While ever to her dear Eulalie upturns her matron eye—
  While ever to her young Eulalie upturns her violet eye.
candidate_text:
Before I met her, every evening
seemed to settle heavily upon the town.
Now one familiar face brings warmth,
and even distant stars appear less cold.
The days have found a softer rhythm;
my restless thoughts no longer wander.
Love has made a home in ordinary hours,
and night no longer feels so vast.

candidate_text:
My days were heavy before she came;
the evening sky seemed distant and cold.
Now her eyes bring light to the room,
and old fears no longer rule my thoughts.
The stars may shine above the rooftops,
but her presence is brighter to me.
I have found a quiet happiness
that makes the world feel whole.

source_title: I will be the gladdest thing
source_text:
Under the sun!
  I will touch a hundred flowers
    And not pick one.

  I will look at cliffs and clouds
    With quiet eyes,
  Watch the wind bow down the grass,
    And the grass rise.

  And when lights begin to show
    Up from the town,
  I will mark which must be mine,
    And then start down!
candidate_text:
I walked outside before the town awoke,
letting the cool air settle on my face.
Wildflowers leaned beside the footpath;
I left them growing where they stood.
Cloud shadows crossed the distant ridge,
and grasses lifted after the breeze.
When evening lamps appeared below,
I turned home slowly, carrying the calm.

candidate_text:
I will spend the day beneath open skies,
touching petals only with my gaze.
I will watch the clouds move over the hills
and see the grass bend, then rise again.
When evening lights appear in the valley,
I will choose the road that leads home.
There is no need to hurry;
the world has given me enough for today.

source_title: Live all thy sweet life through
source_text:
Sweet Rose, dew-sprent,
    Drop down thine evening dew
    To gather it anew
    When day is bright:
      I fancy thou wast meant
    Chiefly to give delight.

    Sing in the silent sky,
      Glad soaring bird;
    Sing out thy notes on high
    To sunbeam straying by
    Or passing cloud;
      Heedless if thou art heard
    Sing thy full song aloud.

    O that it were with me
      As with the flower;
    Blooming on its own tree
    For butterfly and bee
    Its summer morns:
      That I might bloom mine hour
    A rose in spite of thorns.

    O that my work were done
      As birds' that soar
    Rejoicing in the sun:
    That when my time is run
    And daylight too,
      I so might rest once more
    Cool with refreshing dew.
candidate_text:
A rose keeps blooming after sunset,
its petals bright with evening rain.
A bird continues its song above the roofs,
though no one pauses to listen.
I wish my own days held such freedom:
to grow, to sing, and not be measured.
When the light has finished its journey,
may I find rest as quietly as they.

The rose receives the evening rain
and holds its freshness through the night.
A bird sings high above the garden,
whether anyone hears or not.
I long to live with such ease,
to offer what I can while I am here.
When my season comes to its end,
let me rest without regret.

source_title: If I might see another Spring
source_text:
I'd not plant summer flowers and wait:
    I'd have my crocuses at once,
    My leafless pink mezereons,
      My chill-veined snowdrops, choicer yet
      My white or azure violet,
    Leaf-nested primrose; anything
      To blow at once not late.

    If I might see another Spring
      I'd listen to the daylight birds
    That build their nests and pair and sing,
    Nor wait for mateless nightingale;
      I'd listen to the lusty herds,
      The ewes with lambs as white as snow,
    I'd find out music in the hail
      And all the winds that blow.

    If I might see another Spring--
      O stinging comment on my past
    That all my past results in "if"--
      If I might see another Spring
    I'd laugh to-day, to-day is brief;
      I would not wait for anything:
      I'd use to-day that cannot last,
      Be glad to-day and sing.
candidate_text:
If spring returns, I will not postpone
the walks I promised myself last year.
I will hear the nesting birds at sunrise
and watch new leaves unfold along the road.
The season never waits for certainty;
its brief green hours ask to be lived.
So let today be more than preparation:
I will meet it while it is here.

If another spring should come,
I would welcome its flowers without delay.
I would listen to the birds at dawn
and watch the lambs move through the fields.
I would not save every joy for later;
the present hour is already passing.
Let me laugh while the light remains
and use the day that I have been given.

source_title: Helen, thy beauty is to me
source_text:
Like those Nicean barks of yore,
  That gently, o’er a perfumed sea,
    The weary, wayworn wanderer bore
    To his own native shore.

  On desperate seas long wont to roam,
    Thy hyacinth hair, thy classic face,
  Thy Naiad airs have brought me home
    To the glory that was Greece,
  To the grandeur that was Rome.

  Lo! in yon brilliant window niche,
    How statue-like I see thee stand,
    The agate lamp within thy hand!
  Ah, Psyche, from the regions which
    Are Holy Land!
candidate_text:
A distant harbor glimmered in my dream,
its quiet water drawing travelers home.
After years among unfamiliar shores,
I recognized a welcome in one face.
The city lights became familiar stars,
and the long voyage loosened its hold.
Somewhere beyond the evening window,
a gentle presence made the world feel near.

candidate_text:
Like a vessel returning after a long voyage,
I found peace in the sight of your face.
The sea had carried me through distant lands,
but your presence made the journey end.
Your quiet beauty recalled old stories
of home, of art, and ancient cities.
I stood before you as before a statue,
filled with wonder and gratitude.

source_title: Science! true daughter of Old Time thou art!
source_text:
Who alterest all things with thy peering eyes.
  Why preyest thou thus upon the poet’s heart,
    Vulture, whose wings are dull realities?
  How should he love thee? or how deem thee wise,
    Who wouldst not leave him in his wandering
  To seek for treasure in the jewelled skies,
    Albeit he soared with an undaunted wing?
  Hast thou not dragged Diana from her car?
    And driven the Hamadryad from the wood
  To seek a shelter in some happier star?
    Hast thou not torn the Naiad from her flood,
  The Elfin from the green grass, and from me
    The summer dream beneath the tamarind tree?
candidate_text:
The scholar measures every falling star
and names the forces shaping stone.
Yet in the garden, old legends linger:
a river spirit beneath the willow,
a hidden song inside the summer leaves.
Can numbers hold the whole of wonder,
or explain why dreams return at night?
The mind may chart the heavens,
but imagination still gives them wings.

source_title: Science! true daughter of Old Time thou art!
source_text:
Who alterest all things with thy peering eyes.
  Why preyest thou thus upon the poet’s heart,
    Vulture, whose wings are dull realities?
  How should he love thee? or how deem thee wise,
    Who wouldst not leave him in his wandering
  To seek for treasure in the jewelled skies,
    Albeit he soared with an undaunted wing?
  Hast thou not dragged Diana from her car?
    And driven the Hamadryad from the wood
  To seek a shelter in some happier star?
    Hast thou not torn the Naiad from her flood,
  The Elfin from the green grass, and from me
    The summer dream beneath the tamarind tree?
candidate_text:
You look at the world through measured glass
and strip the mystery from every tale.
The poet once found spirits in the river,
and heard old gods among the trees.
Now the names of wonder disappear,
replaced by facts and careful diagrams.
Still, a dream survives beyond the numbers;
not every truth can be weighed.

source_text:
Sonnets

  I
       Thou art not lovelier than lilacs,--no,

  II
       Time does not bring relief; you all have lied

  III
       Mindful of you the sodden earth in spring,

  IV
       Not in this chamber only at my birth--

  V
       If I should learn, in some quite casual way,

  VI     Bluebeard
       This door you might not open, and you did;
candidate_text:
A quiet garden keeps its secrets
beneath the branches after rain.
A stranger passes through the flowers,
then disappears beyond the lane.

I keep the memory of that visit,
not knowing whether it was real.
Some moments leave no footprints,
yet remain in everything we feel.

A visitor once appeared inside a walled garden.
She moved among the flowers with a graceful manner

source_text:
Loud he sang the psalm of David!
He, a Negro and enslaved,
Sang of Israel's victory,
Sang of Zion, bright and free.

In that hour, when night is calmest,
Sang he from the Hebrew Psalmist,
In a voice so sweet and clear
That I could not choose but hear,

Songs of triumph, and ascriptions,
Such as reached the swart Egyptians,
When upon the Red Sea coast
Perished Pharaoh and his host.

And the voice of his devotion
Filled my soul with strange emotion;
For its tones by turns were glad,
Sweetly solemn, wildly sad.

Paul and Silas, in their prison,
Sang of Christ, the Lord arisen,
And an earthquake's arm of might
Broke their dungeon-gates at night.

But, alas! what holy angel
Brings the Slave this glad evangel?
And what earthquake's arm of might
Breaks his dungeon-gates at night?
candidate_text:
A voice rose from a locked room
while midnight covered the sleeping street.
The song carried stories of distant freedom,
and courage answered from the dark.
Those who listened stood without speaking;
their hearts were stirred by every note.
The singer still faced an iron door,
but the melody traveled beyond it.

At midnight a prisoner began to sing,
his voice rising above the walls.
He sang of a people crossing the sea,
of chains broken and a home regained.
The sound reached those who kept watch,

Yet when the song had ended,

source_text:
WHEN I go up through the mowing field,
    The headless aftermath,
    Smooth-laid like thatch with the heavy dew,
    Half closes the garden path.
    And when I come to the garden ground,
    The whir of sober birds
    Up from the tangle of withered weeds
    Is sadder than any words.
    A tree beside the wall stands bare,
    But a leaf that lingered brown,
    Disturbed, I doubt not, by my thought,
    Comes softly rattling down.
    I end not far from my going forth
    By picking the faded blue
    Of the last remaining aster flower
    To carry again to you.
candidate_text:
I crossed the field after harvest,
where damp grass bent beneath my steps.
A few birds called from the hedge,
then vanished into the fading light.
One brown leaf loosened from a branch
and spun across the garden path.
I found a small blue flower near the wall
and carried its color back to you.

Birds rose suddenly from the weeds,

source_text:
WHEN the wind works against us in the dark,
    And pelts with snow
    The lowest chamber window on the east,
    And whispers with a sort of stifled bark,
    The beast,
    'Come out! Come out!'--
    It costs no inward struggle not to go,
    Ah, no!
    I count our strength,
    Two and a child,
    Those of us not asleep subdued to mark
    How the cold creeps as the fire dies at length,--
    How drifts are piled,
    Dooryard and road ungraded,
    Till even the comforting barn grows far away
    And my heart owns a doubt
    Whether 'tis in us to arise with day
    And save ourselves unaided.
candidate_text:
The storm pressed hard against the windows,
and snow covered the road before night.
Inside, we counted blankets and candles,
keeping close while the fire grew low.
The house creaked beneath the weather;
the barn seemed farther with every gust.
We waited for the dark to loosen,
trusting the morning would bring a way.

Wind drove the snow against the eastern window,
while the house grew colder after dark.
We stayed together by the dying fire,
counting the hours until morning.
The road and barn disappeared beneath drifts;

I wondered whether we could face the day,
but held my family close through the storm.

source_text:
To Mercy, Pity, Peace, and Love,
     All pray in their distress,
   And to these virtues of delight
     Return their thankfulness.

   For Mercy, Pity, Peace, and Love,
     Is God our Father dear;
   And Mercy, Pity, Peace, and Love,
     Is man, his child and care.

   For Mercy has a human heart
     Pity, a human face;
   And Love, the human form divine;
     And Peace, the human dress.

   Then every man, of every clime,
     That prays in his distress,
   Prays to the human form divine:
     Love, Mercy, Pity, Peace.

   And all must love the human form,
     In heathen, Turk, or Jew.
   Where Mercy, Love, and Pity dwell,
     There God is dwelling too.
candidate_text:
When people suffer, they seek compassion,
a patient hand and words that soothe.
Kindness gives a face to mercy;
peace can live in how we treat a stranger.
Across the borders people draw,
the same need for care remains.
Where love is offered without condition,
a little light enters the world.

Compassion lives in a human gesture,

Where patience and tenderness remain,

source_text:
The sun descending in the west,
   The evening star does shine;
   The birds are silent in their nest,
   And I must seek for mine.
     The moon, like a flower
     In heaven's high bower,
     With silent delight,
     Sits and smiles on the night.

   Farewell, green fields and happy grove,
   Where flocks have ta'en delight.
   Where lambs have nibbled, silent move
   The feet of angels bright;
     Unseen they pour blessing,
     And joy without ceasing,
     On each bud and blossom,
     And each sleeping bosom.

   They look in every thoughtless nest
   Where birds are covered warm;
   They visit caves of every beast,
   To keep them all from harm:
     If they see any weeping
     That should have been sleeping,
     They pour sleep on their head,
     And sit down by their bed.

   When wolves and tigers howl for prey,
   They pitying stand and weep;
   Seeking to drive their thirst away,
   And keep them from the sheep.
     But, if they rush dreadful,
     The angels, most heedful,
     Receive each mild spirit,
     New worlds to inherit.
candidate_text:
The last light slips behind the hills,
and birds settle among the branches.
A pale moon rises over the fields,
watching the quiet village below.
Small creatures rest beneath the leaves;
night air moves gently through the grass.
May every tired heart find shelter
until the morning opens once again.

May the weary find their shelter,
and wake beneath a kinder sky.
